title: Wicket and the Whispering Leaf
markdown:
In days long vanished, high in the Skytusk Archipelago, where mountains clawed the sky and rope ferries trembled over water like black glass, lived a wizard named Tobin. His days were usually quiet: lichens catalogued, charms perfected, purple robes kept free of thyme. His companion was a donkey named Wicket, who possessed a quiet wisdom his master often missed, and who had a habit of looking into still pools as if the mountains might answer there.

Tobin yearned, more than he admitted, to be seen as the sort of wizard who knew every secret the peaks kept. Not merely competent. Impressive. Reflected in other people’s eyes as a man of passage and weather and fate.

The wish arrived as a halted ferry. Lord Elmsworth, thoroughly ruffled, found him.

“Wizard Tobin?” Voice tight.

Tobin puffed his chest. “Indeed, my Lord. Passage through the treacherous peaks to the Obsidian Spire? A simple matter.” He had conveniently forgotten the blizzard that had grounded the usual sky-carts. The ferry’s cables hummed. Below, the water held a ruffled lord and a puffed wizard, both looking slightly less grand than they intended.

Wicket blinked. A soft hee-haw suggested doubt.

The bargain was struck without anyone calling it a bargain. Elmsworth needed a guide. Tobin needed an audience. Wicket needed thyme, which he found, and munched.

“These mountains hold secrets,” Tobin whispered, conspiratorial, leaning in. “I know them all.” He straightened the deep purple robes and gave Wicket a stern look. “No dawdling. We present a united front.”

Wicket’s large eyes observed with calm patience. Elmsworth sighed, wishing he had stayed on the ferry, where at least the water had been honest.

First boon: they set out. Tobin strode ahead, pointing dramatically at clouds.

“Cumulonimbus formations mean swift passage. No concern.”

Wicket was the true navigator. He nudged Tobin’s pack toward stable ground and steered him from slippery scree. Long shadows, like a tiger’s stripes, danced across the path. The first consequence was subtle: Tobin’s pronouncements arrived a beat after Wicket’s hooves had already chosen. Elmsworth noticed. Tobin did not, being busy with the sky.

Then a raspy voice. “Trinkets. Shiny things.”

A goblin, Fobble, coal-chip eyes, clutching peculiar goods. Tobin cleared his throat.

“Fobble. A sprig of Moonpetal Bloom. For a delicate constitution.”

Elmsworth clutched his cloak, expecting an ambush. Second boon: a rare herb, or so Tobin wished it to be, a charm to make the lord’s journey as smooth as his own reflection in a breakfast spoon.

Fobble cackled, rattling pebbles. “Moonpetal? Got something rarer.” With a flourish he produced a large spiky pinecone. “For your delicate constitution.” He thrust it at Elmsworth. The pinecone snagged velvet, tearing a gaping rip.

Mirror twist: the delicate constitution was the cloak. Dignity, tattered. Wind found the hole and made a small rude music.

“Oh, dear,” Tobin muttered, facade crumbling. Vanity pricked. Hands trembled. Elmsworth looked crestfallen.

Then Wicket stepped forward. He nudged Elmsworth gently, trotted to a thicket, and returned with a large velvety leaf. Using his muzzle, he tucked it into the rip and smoothed it down. Third boon, not Tobin’s: a leaf that kept the wind at bay. The major reversal was quiet. No sparks. No spells. Practical kindness, reflected in Elmsworth’s face more kindly than any charm.

“Well, I’ll be,” Tobin whispered.

Elmsworth smiled, patting Wicket’s head. “A very sensible solution, my dear donkey. Far more useful than any hasty charm.” A genuine chuckle.

A blush crept up Tobin’s neck. Grand pronouncements, overshadowed by a leaf.

“My apologies, my Lord. I may have overestimated my preparedness. Wicket, however… you see the wisdom of a true companion.” He looked at Wicket with newfound respect. Atonement, if not a speech.

They continued. Mist swirled. The obsidian spire glinted, a dark mirror of the sky. It was not Tobin’s prowess Elmsworth would remember. It was the gentle nudge of a donkey, and a leaf that knew more about wind than a wizard who had wished to know everything. Wicket, for his part, found more thyme, and did not gloat, which was another kind of wisdom, and rarer.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, highland fantasy adventure for teens
